subtype: Approach: doing the hardest tasks personally to be safe [Pitfall]
passage:
Vinita: So what went wrong on your first project?

Girish: I'm Girish. I was the youngest man they'd ever made lead. I was scared of mistakes, so I kept every hard module: payments, data migration, the security parts. I told myself it was quicker to do it right myself. I stayed until midnight for weeks. Meanwhile Charu, who could easily have handled the migration, waited for small tickets and drew doodles in her notebook. Everything queued up behind me. The deadline slipped by two weeks, and the client was not pleased. Only later did I see that it wasn't diligence. It was fear. I had made myself the bottleneck, and the team was sitting idle.

qa.q: Until what time did Girish stay at work?
qa.a: Girish stayed until midnight for weeks.
Girish was afraid of making mistakes, which was why he kept every hard module.

qa.q: What could Girish have done differently, and why?
qa.a: Girish could have handed one hard module to a teammate like Charu and reviewed it together, because sharing the load stops one person from becoming the bottleneck.

qa.q: How might Charu have felt during those weeks?
qa.a: Charu probably felt underused and frustrated, waiting for small tickets while capable of more.

grounding: Illustrates a new lead keeping every hard task for himself out of fear, which leaves teammates idle and slips the deadline.

subtype: Approach: doing the hardest tasks personally to be safe [Pitfall]
passage:
I'm Divyansh, on Uday's team at the fintech office. When Uday became lead in March, he took every hard module himself: the payment engine, the fraud checks, the reconciliation. He said, "If something breaks, I want it to be my mistake."
The rest of us got small tickets. I spent a week changing button colours. Meenakshi, who'd built payment systems before, fixed typos in documentation.
By April Uday was leaving at eleven every night. Code reviews for our small tasks waited days because he had no time. In stand-ups he looked grey.
In May the release date came and went. The payment engine wasn't done. Our manager asked why nobody else had worked on it. Uday said quietly, "I didn't want to risk it."
I can't say exactly what he felt, but he looked like someone who had carried everything and dropped it anyway.

qa.q: What did Meenakshi do while Uday handled the hard modules?
What was Uday feeling when he kept every hard module?
qa.a: He felt afraid of mistakes, wanting any failure to be his own, which led him to hold on to everything.

qa.q: What approach would have suited Uday better as a new lead?
qa.a: Sharing the hard modules with experienced teammates like Meenakshi and reviewing their work would have spread the load and kept the release on track.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Divyansh?
qa.a: Divyansh feels underused changing button colours and sees Uday grow exhausted, becoming the bottleneck that delays everyone.

grounding: Shows a new lead keeping every difficult module for himself out of fear, working late while teammates sit idle, and missing the deadline.

subtype: Approach: doing the hardest tasks personally to be safe [Pitfall]
passage:
Week one. Chaitanya was made lead of a five-person team building a new booking system. He looked at the list and thought, the search engine and the pricing logic are the hardest. If someone else gets them wrong, I'll look bad. So he took both. Gurleen, who had built pricing logic at her last job, got the login page.
Week four. Chaitanya was at the office past midnight most days. The others finished their small tasks early and waited for his reviews. Gurleen offered twice to help with pricing. "I've got it," he said.
Week eight. Launch week. Search worked; pricing didn't. Gurleen's login page had been finished for a month. The manager postponed the launch by three weeks. In the meeting, Chaitanya stared at the table.
Afterwards Gurleen said gently, "You don't have to carry it all." He nodded, too tired to answer.

qa.q: How long was the launch postponed?
qa.a: The launch was postponed by three weeks.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya keep both hard modules, and how was he feeling?
qa.a: He was afraid of looking bad if someone else got them wrong, so he held on to them out of fear and ended up exhausted.

qa.q: What would you change first in Chaitanya's plan?
qa.a: I would give the pricing logic to Gurleen, who had built it before, and review her work, so the hardest parts move in parallel.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel during those eight weeks?
qa.a: Gurleen likely felt underused and a bit frustrated, finishing early and having her offers to help turned down.

grounding: Shows a new lead keeping the hardest modules for himself out of fear, becoming the bottleneck while skilled teammates sit underused, and missing the launch.
